A.q: Was the thinking machine conceived in theory before any computer existed to run it?

B.q: Was AI already up and running before Dartmouth named it in 1956?
articles: A Talk on the Third Programme
books: When the Field Got Its Name

C.q: Did the first AI winter prove that the field's early promises had outrun its science?

D.q: Did the 1980s boom and the second winter show AI caught in a cycle of hype and collapse?

cards.title: Turing Writes to Ashby About the ACE
cards.content: A two-page signed letter from the National Physical Laboratory to the psychiatrist W. Ross Ashby, discussing the planned ACE computer.
cards.significance: Turing confides he is more interested in producing models of the action of the brain than in practical computing, and urges Ashby to run his experiments on the ACE - the brain-modelling ambition stated privately a decade before the field had a name.
cards.author: Alan M. Turing
cards.citation: W. Ross Ashby Digital Archive (ashby.info), scan courtesy of the National Physical Laboratory; carbon copy in the Turing Archive for the History of Computing, item L23-001
cards.quote: "In working on the ACE I am more interested in the possibility of producing models of the action of the brain than in the practical applications of computing."
cards.imageCredit: Turing, Alan M. Letter to W. Ross Ashby, ca. November 19, 1946. Digitized scan, courtesy of the National Physical Laboratory. The W. Ross Ashby Digital Archive. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://ashby.info/letters/images/wralx018.jpg.

cards.title: Ashby's Journal
cards.content: A continuously dated private working notebook of some 7,400 pages recording Ashby's ideas on brains and machines across 44 years.
cards.significance: Entry by dated entry, the journal shows a member of the Turing-Wiener circle working out the homeostat and his design for a brain - a question set in 1928, decades before the field existed, and answered across the era this deck opens with.
cards.author: W. Ross Ashby
cards.citation: British Library, Add MS 89153/1-25 (Papers of William Ross Ashby); complete page images in the W. Ross Ashby Digital Archive (ashby.info)
cards.quote: "Today I can say I have solved the problem I set out to solve on 7 May '28. I asked, roughly, whence come the patterning properties of the nervous system. The answer is now clear." (entry of June 13, 1959)
cards.imageCredit: Ashby, W. Ross. Journal, pages 6116-6117, entry of June 13, 1959. Digitized page image. The W. Ross Ashby Digital Archive; original in Add MS 89153, British Library, London. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://ashby.info/journal/page/images/wrac3180.jpg.

cards.title: Turing's Lecture to the London Mathematical Society
cards.content: The typescript of a public lecture on the Automatic Computing Engine and the prospect of machines that learn from experience.
cards.significance: The first public lecture on computer intelligence: Turing told a mathematical audience that a machine should be allowed to make mistakes and to learn like a pupil, two years before any British stored-program computer ran.
cards.author: Alan M. Turing
cards.citation: Xerox of Turing's typescript with additions, item AMT/B/1, Turing Papers, King's College Archive Centre, Cambridge; first published 1986 (Carpenter and Doran, eds., MIT Press)
cards.quote: "What we want is a machine that can learn from experience."
cards.imageCredit: Chaffin, Arthur Reginald (attributed). Alan Turing Aged 16. 1928-1929. Photograph. Public domain; related material in the Turing Papers, King's College Archive Centre, Cambridge. Wikimedia Commons. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a1/Alan_Turing_Aged_16.jpg.

cards.title: On Computable Numbers
cards.content: A mathematical paper read to the London Mathematical Society, defining the computable numbers and the universal computing machine.
cards.significance: The theoretical foundation of all computing: Turing's imagined universal machine proved on paper that one device could carry out any computation - the thinking machine conceived in logic a decade before electronics could attempt it.
cards.author: A. M. Turing
cards.citation: Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society, ser. 2, 42 (1936-37): 230-265; received May 28, 1936, read November 12, 1936; corrections in ser. 2, 43 (1937)
cards.quote: "The "computable" numbers may be described briefly as the real numbers whose expressions as a decimal are calculable by finite means."
cards.imageCredit: Turing, A. M. "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem." First page. Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society, ser. 2, 42 (1936-37): 230-265. Page scan hosted by the University of Virginia. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://www.cs.virginia.edu/~robins/Turing_Paper_1936.pdf.

cards.title: Programming the ENIAC
cards.content: A U.S. Army photograph of programmers Jean Jennings Bartik and Frances Bilas Spence operating the ENIAC at the Moore School of Electrical Engineering.
cards.significance: The first general-purpose electronic computer and the women who programmed it: the machine whose 1946 press debut planted the phrase "electronic brain" - the hardware precondition for every thinking-machine claim that followed.
cards.author: U.S. Army (photographer unidentified)
cards.citation: U.S. Army photograph, 1946, from the archives of the ARL Technical Library; record published by the National Women's History Museum via Google Arts and Culture; public-domain file on Wikimedia Commons
cards.quote: "Two women operating ENIAC" (catalogue caption)
cards.imageCredit: U.S. Army. Two Women Operating ENIAC. 1946. Photograph, photographer unidentified; from the archives of the ARL Technical Library. Public domain. Wikimedia Commons. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8c/Two_women_operating_ENIAC_%28full_resolution%29.jpg.

cards.title: Richardson's Forecast-Factory Map
cards.content: The frontispiece map of Richardson's treatise on computing the weather, dividing Europe into a chessboard of alternating pressure and momentum cells.
cards.significance: Computation imagined before computers: Richardson dreamed of a "forecast-factory" of 64,000 human computers racing the weather - the organized-calculation vision that ENIAC's 1950 forecasts, run by von Neumann's team, finally redeemed.
cards.author: Lewis Fry Richardson
cards.citation: Richardson, Weather Prediction by Numerical Process (Cambridge University Press, 1922), frontispiece; complete scan at the Internet Archive
cards.quote: "Perhaps some day in the dim future it will be possible to advance the computations faster than the weather advances and at a cost less than the saving to mankind due to the information gained. But that is a dream."
cards.imageCredit: Richardson, Lewis Fry. Weather Prediction by Numerical Process. Frontispiece map. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1922. Public domain. Internet Archive. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://archive.org/details/weatherpredictio00richrich.

cards.title: The Mechanical Brain
cards.content: A news report on the Manchester University computer, carrying Professor Geoffrey Jefferson's doubts and a telephone interview with Alan Turing in reply.
cards.significance: The first newspaper debate over a thinking machine: the Jefferson-Turing argument that began in the Lister Oration reached the public on this page, with Turing promising far more to come.
cards.author: Our Special Correspondent (The Times, London)
cards.citation: The Times (London), June 11, 1949, p. 4; The Times Digital Archive (Gale); wording corroborated by the Quote Investigator analysis of the Gale scan
cards.quote: "This is only a foretaste of what is to come, and only the shadow of what is going to be." (Turing, as quoted in the article)
cards.imageCredit: "The Mechanical Brain: Answer Found to 300 Year-Old Sum." The Times (London), June 11, 1949, 4. The Times Digital Archive (Gale); wording corroborated at quoteinvestigator.com/2019/10/12/ai-shadow/. Accessed November 10, 2026.

cards.title: Von Neumann Writes Wiener on Brains and Automata
cards.content: A seven-page letter from the Institute for Advanced Study to Norbert Wiener at MIT on automata and the nervous system, ahead of a meeting of their research circle.
cards.significance: Two central figures of the founding circle privately weighing where machine-brain research should go, including von Neumann's doubts about the McCulloch-Pitts route and his case for studying self-reproducing systems first.
cards.author: John von Neumann
cards.citation: Norbert Wiener papers, MC-0022, MIT Libraries Distinctive Collections; copy catalogued in the Heinz von Foerster Archive, University of Vienna; published in Redei, ed., John von Neumann: Selected Letters (2005)
cards.quote: "After the great positive contribution of Turing-cum-Pitts-and-McCulloch is assimilated, the situation is rather worse than better than before."
cards.imageCredit: Los Alamos National Laboratory. John von Neumann. N.d. Identification-badge photograph. LANL (attribution requested). Wikimedia Commons. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5e/JohnvonNeumann-LosAlamos.gif.

cards.title: Tootill's Manchester Notebook
cards.content: The laboratory notebook Geoff Tootill kept at Manchester while building the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, with dated program workings from the summer of 1948.
cards.significance: The only contemporary record of the world's first stored-program computer running: its page of July 18, 1948 preserves Kilburn's highest-factor routine as amended - the program family with which the "Baby" made its first run that June 21.
cards.author: Geoff C. Tootill
cards.citation: Archive of the Science and Industry Museum, Manchester; page images and account published by the University of Manchester's Computer50 and Digital 60 projects
cards.quote: "Kilburn Highest Factor Routine (amended)" (notebook heading of July 18, 1948)
cards.imageCredit: Tootill, Geoff C. Notebook page, "Kilburn Highest Factor Routine (amended)," July 18, 1948. Page image. University of Manchester Computer50 archive; original notebook in the archive of the Science and Industry Museum, Manchester. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://curation.cs.manchester.ac.uk/computer50/www.computer50.org/kgill/mark1/prog.gif.

cards.title: The Mind of Mechanical Man
cards.content: The Lister Oration delivered to the Royal College of Surgeons by Manchester's professor of neurosurgery, published in the British Medical Journal.
cards.significance: The founding statement of machine-intelligence skepticism: Jefferson's sonnet test drew Turing's reply in the Times that week and again in his 1950 paper - the critics' argument stated before the field existed.
cards.author: Sir Geoffrey Jefferson
cards.citation: British Medical Journal 1, no. 4616 (June 25, 1949): 1105-1110; PubMed Central PMC2050428
cards.quote: "Not until a machine can write a sonnet or compose a concerto because of thoughts and emotions felt, and not by the chance fall of symbols, could we agree that machine equals brain-that is, not only write it but know that it had written it."
cards.imageCredit: Jefferson, Geoffrey. "The Mind of Mechanical Man." First page. British Medical Journal 1, no. 4616 (June 25, 1949): 1105-1110. PubMed Central PMC2050428. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2050428/.

cards.title: Maelzel's Chess-Player
cards.content: A magazine essay analyzing the celebrated chess-playing "automaton" exhibited by Johann Maelzel, arguing from seventeen observations that a hidden human directs every move.
cards.significance: The archetypal expose of a thinking-machine scam: the Turk toured courts and theaters for seven decades as a machine that played chess, and Poe reasoned his way to the concealed operator a doctrine before the secret was published.
cards.author: Edgar Allan Poe
cards.citation: Southern Literary Messenger 2 (April 1836): 318-326; full text, Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore (eapoe.org)
cards.quote: "It is quite certain that the operations of the Automaton are regulated by mind, and by nothing else."
cards.imageCredit: Poe, Edgar Allan. "Maelzel's Chess-Player." First page, p. 318. Southern Literary Messenger 2, no. 5 (April 1836): 318-326. Issue scan, Internet Archive; full-text edition, Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://archive.org/details/sim_southern-literary-messenger_1836-04_2_5.

cards.title: Mr. von Osten and Clever Hans
cards.content: The frontispiece photograph of Pfungst's experimental study: Wilhelm von Osten in his white coat beside the horse Hans, with the arithmetic blackboards used in the famous demonstrations.
cards.significance: The era's great illusory-intelligence case: crowds and committees believed a horse could calculate, until Pfungst's blindfold tests showed Hans was reading involuntary human cues - a lesson in credulous observers that AI testing keeps relearning.
cards.author: Oskar Pfungst (frontispiece to his study)
cards.citation: Frontispiece, Oskar Pfungst, Clever Hans (The Horse of Mr. von Osten), trans. C. L. Rahn (New York: Henry Holt, 1911); full text and plates, Project Gutenberg No. 33936
cards.quote: "The proof which was expected by so many, that animals possess the power of thought, was not furnished by Hans" (the study's verdict; the photograph is its frontispiece)
cards.imageCredit: Frontispiece photograph: Mr. von Osten and Hans. In Oskar Pfungst, Clever Hans (The Horse of Mr. von Osten), trans. Carl L. Rahn. New York: Henry Holt, 1911. Public domain. Project Gutenberg No. 33936. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://www.gutenberg.org/files/33936/33936-h/images/frontispiece.jpg.

cards.title: Inside the Turk: Racknitz's Cutaway
cards.content: A hand-colored engraved cross-section of Kempelen's chess automaton, charting how a concealed player could sit inside the cabinet behind the display of clockwork.
cards.significance: A map of the scam's interior drawn while the scam still toured: Racknitz's conjectured plan - hidden operator, candle, false machinery - was published sixty-five years before the Turk's secret was formally revealed.
cards.author: Joseph Friedrich, Freiherr zu Racknitz
cards.citation: Racknitz, Ueber den Schachspieler des Herrn von Kempelen und dessen Nachbildung (Leipzig and Dresden: Breitkopf, 1789), Tab. III; institutional scan at the University of Rostock; plate images via Humboldt University Library on Wikimedia Commons
cards.quote: "Ueber den Schachspieler des Herrn von Kempelen und dessen Nachbildung" (title; the plate is Tab. III)
cards.imageCredit: Racknitz, Joseph Friedrich zu. Tab. III. In Ueber den Schachspieler des Herrn von Kempelen und dessen Nachbildung. Leipzig and Dresden: Breitkopf, 1789. Hand-colored engraving. Public domain, via Humboldt University Library; institutional scan at the University of Rostock (PURL purl.uni-rostock.de/rosdok/ppn1842789147). Wikimedia Commons. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6e/Racknitz_-_The_Turk_3.jpg.

cards.title: An Electronic Brain
cards.content: The Times's report of Lord Mountbatten's address to the British Institution of Radio Engineers the night before, announcing that the stage was set to evolve an "electronic brain."
cards.significance: The founding artifact of modern AI misinformation: radio valves "activating each other in the way brain cells do," machines taking on "choice and judgment," even "a rather mediocre game of chess" - the coverage Hartree's letter corrected six days later.
cards.author: Unsigned (The Times, London)
cards.citation: The Times (London), November 1, 1946 ("An Electronic Brain: Solving Abstruse Problems; Valves with a Memory"); The Times Digital Archive (Gale); page captures in the project gallery
cards.quote: "The stage was now set for "the most Wellsian development of all." It was considered possible to evolve an electronic brain, which would perform functions analogous to those at present undertaken by the semi-automatic portions of the human brain."
cards.imageCredit: "An Electronic Brain: Solving Abstruse Problems; Valves with a Memory." The Times (London), November 1, 1946. The Times Digital Archive (Gale). Accessed November 10, 2026.

cards.title: Hartree Corrects the "Electronic Brain"
cards.content: A letter to the editor of The Times from the Cambridge professor who had run the ENIAC, objecting to press descriptions of the new calculating machines as "electronic brains."
cards.significance: The first public correction of modern AI misinformation: within a week of the term's debut, the man who best knew the machines wrote that they could do only what their operators set up - beginning a correction cycle that never ended.
cards.author: Douglas R. Hartree
cards.citation: The Times (London), November 7, 1946, p. 5; wording verified in Goncalves, Philosophy and Technology 36 (2023), open access; The Times Digital Archive (Gale)
cards.quote: "These machines can only do precisely what they are instructed to do by the operators who set them up."
cards.imageCredit: Hartree, D. R. "The 'Electronic Brain': A Misleading Term." Letter to the editor. The Times (London), November 7, 1946, 5. The Times Digital Archive (Gale). Accessed November 10, 2026.

cards.title: The EDSAC Log Book
cards.content: The operations log book of the Cambridge Mathematical Laboratory's EDSAC, opened the day the machine first ran.
cards.significance: The working diary of the first practical stored-program computer: day by dated day it records the machine, its faults, and the moment electronic computing became a service to science - the workbench on which the birth era's programs ran.
cards.author: Mathematical Laboratory, University of Cambridge
cards.citation: University of Cambridge Mathematical Laboratory; opening pages transcribed on the Computer Laboratory's Relics site; photograph of the first page at the Centre for Computing History, Cambridge (CH51856)
cards.quote: "Machine in operation for first time. Printed table of squares (0-99), time for programme 2 mins. 35 secs." (entry of May 6, 1949)
cards.imageCredit: Handwritten Log Showing First Successful Run of EDSAC. May 6, 1949. Photographic print, Peter Bird collection. Reference CH51856, Centre for Computing History, Cambridge. Accessed November 10, 2026. http://www.computinghistory.org.uk/det/51856/51856-EDSAC-log.

cards.title: Can Digital Computers Think?
cards.content: The typescript of Turing's radio talk on the BBC Third Programme, asking whether digital computers could be said to think.
cards.significance: Turing taking the machine-intelligence question to a national radio audience five years before Dartmouth - with his warning about machines that might come to outthink their makers.
cards.author: Alan M. Turing
cards.citation: BBC Third Programme, May 15, 1951; annotated typescript item AMT/B/5, Turing Papers, King's College Archive Centre, Cambridge; transcript published via The Aperiodical
cards.quote: "If a machine can think, it might think more intelligently than we do, and then where should we be?"
cards.imageCredit: Turing, Alan M. "Can Digital Computers Think?" Annotated typescript, 1951. Item AMT/B/5, Turing Papers, King's College Archive Centre, Cambridge. The Turing Digital Archive. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://turingarchive.kings.cam.ac.uk/publications-lectures-and-talks-amtb/amt-b-5.

cards.title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
cards.content: A philosophy-journal article proposing the imitation game as a practical substitute for the question whether machines can think.
cards.significance: The Turing test's source document: the most cited paper in the history of machine intelligence, answering Jefferson's objections point by point and predicting machines that learn - the birth era's intellectual charter.
cards.author: A. M. Turing
cards.quote: "I propose to consider the question, "Can machines think?""
cards.imageCredit: Turing, A. M. "Computing Machinery and Intelligence." Mind 59, no. 236 (October 1950): 433-460. Full-text transcription. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://courses.cs.umbc.edu/471/papers/turing.pdf.

cards.title: Shannon and Theseus in the Maze
cards.content: A publicity photograph of Claude Shannon guiding his relay-driven electric mouse, Theseus, through its maze at Bell Laboratories.
cards.significance: Theseus was the era's most visible learning machine; this widely reproduced image made Shannon the public face of machine intelligence four years before the field had a name.
cards.author: Bell Telephone Laboratories (publicity photograph)
cards.citation: Computer History Museum, catalog 102630790, lot X7413.2015; the maze itself survives in the MIT Museum
cards.quote: "Claude Shannon moving his electric mouse in a maze." (catalogue caption)
cards.imageCredit: "Nickknack00." Theseus (1950), Betty and Claude Shannon, MIT Museum. 2026. Photograph. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8a/Theseus_%281950%29%2C_Betty_and_Claude_Shannon%2C_MIT_Museum.jpg.

cards.title: The First Computer Weather Maps
cards.content: Contoured 500-millibar forecast charts of North America, observed and machine-computed, published with the report of the first weather forecasts run on ENIAC.
cards.significance: The first forecast maps ever produced by an electronic computer, from the Princeton project von Neumann built to prove his stored-program machine could take on problems once reserved for human judgment - Richardson's dream made electronic.
cards.author: Jule Charney, Ragnar Fjortoft, John von Neumann
cards.citation: Published in Tellus 2(4):237-254 (1950), Swedish Geophysical Society; DOI 10.1111/j.2153-3490.1950.tb00336.x
cards.quote: "the computation time for a 24-hour forecast was about 24 hours, that is, we were just able to keep pace with the weather"
cards.imageCredit: U.S. Army. Glen Beck and Betty Snyder Program the ENIAC in Building 328 at the Ballistic Research Laboratory. Ca. 1947. Photograph, photographer unknown. Public domain. Wikimedia Commons. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d3/Glen_Beck_and_Betty_Snyder_program_the_ENIAC_in_building_328_at_the_Ballistic_Research_Laboratory.jpg.

cards.title: Russian Is Turned Into English
cards.content: A front-page news report of the Georgetown-IBM demonstration at which an IBM 701 translated Russian sentences into English.
cards.significance: Machine translation's public debut and the first computing-with-language spectacle: the demonstration's promises helped open the funding stream that the ALPAC report would shut off twelve years later.
cards.author: Robert K. Plumb
cards.citation: The New York Times, January 8, 1954, p. 1; full transcription in the Machine Translation Archive (ACL Anthology)
cards.quote: "A public demonstration of what is believed to be the first successful use of a machine to translate meaningful texts from one language to another took place here yesterday afternoon."
cards.imageCredit: Plumb, Robert K. "Russian Is Turned Into English by a Fast Electronic Translator." New York Times, January 8, 1954, 1. Transcription, Machine Translation Archive via the ACL Anthology. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://aclanthology.org/www.mt-archive.info/NYT-1954-Plumb.pdf.

cards.title: Strachey Reports His Draughts Program
cards.content: A typed letter to Turing, written the evening of Turing's BBC broadcast, reporting progress on Strachey's draughts program for the Manchester machine.
cards.significance: Game-playing AI's first working correspondence: Strachey's draughts program became the era's most ambitious piece of programming, and this letter ties it directly to Turing's broadcast question.
cards.author: Christopher Strachey
cards.citation: Item AMT/D/5, Turing Papers, King's College Archive Centre, Cambridge; Strachey's carbon in the Strachey Papers, Bodleian Library; quoted in Resurrection 60 (Computer Conservation Society, 2012)
cards.quote: "I am convinced that the crux of problem of learning is recognizing relationships and being able to use them. Of course there is a large amount of matter which has to be simply remembered in the form of facts - the multiplication table, for instance, or the words of the language - but without the assistance of a scheme of relations this knowledge is not much use."
cards.imageCredit: Strachey, Christopher. Letter to Alan Turing, May 15, 1951. Item AMT/D/5, Turing Papers, King's College Archive Centre, Cambridge. The Turing Digital Archive. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://turingarchive.kings.cam.ac.uk/correspondence-amtd/amt-d-5.

cards.title: Solomonoff's Dartmouth Notebook
cards.content: A participant's handwritten notebook and dated daily notes kept through the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project.
cards.significance: Solomonoff was one of the few people present for the whole summer; his dated notes are the principal surviving day-by-day record of the workshop where artificial intelligence got its name.
cards.author: Ray Solomonoff
cards.citation: Solomonoff estate collection; complete scans published at raysolomonoff.com, Dartmouth section
cards.quote: "This idea may, indeed, work."
cards.imageCredit: Solomonoff, Ray. Dartmouth Summer Research Project notebook and notes, 1956. Digitized scans. Ray Solomonoff memorial website, Solomonoff estate. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://raysolomonoff.com/dartmouth/dart.html.

cards.title: Intelligent Machinery, A Heretical Theory
cards.content: The typescript of a talk to Manchester's '51 Society arguing that machines could be made to think, and imagining where that might lead.
cards.significance: Turing's most far-reaching speculation - machine learning, machine conversation, and machines that outstrip their makers - delivered to a private discussion society and unpublished in his lifetime.
cards.author: Alan M. Turing
cards.citation: Typescripts, items AMT/B/4 and AMT/B/20, Turing Papers, King's College Archive Centre, Cambridge; published in The Essential Turing (Oxford, 2004)
cards.quote: ""You cannot make a machine to think for you". This is a commonplace that is usually accepted without question. It will be the purpose of this paper to question it."
cards.imageCredit: Turing, Alan M. "Intelligent Machinery, A Heretical Theory." Typescript, c. 1951. Item AMT/B/4, Turing Papers, King's College Archive Centre, Cambridge. The Turing Digital Archive. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://turingarchive.kings.cam.ac.uk/publications-lectures-and-talks-amtb/amt-b-4.

cards.title: A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence
cards.content: A 17-page typescript proposing a two-month, ten-man summer study of "artificial intelligence" at Dartmouth College.
cards.significance: The document that named the field: the first known use of the term artificial intelligence, closing the birth era by christening what Turing, Shannon, and Strachey had already begun.
cards.author: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, Claude Shannon
cards.citation: Typescript copies in Dartmouth College's Rauner Special Collections and the Stanford McCarthy papers; reprinted in AI Magazine 27(4), 2006
cards.quote: "The study is to proceed on the basis of the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it."
cards.imageCredit: McCarthy, John, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon. "A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence," 1955. Scan of typescript materials, including Ray Solomonoff's signed copy. Ray Solomonoff memorial website. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://raysolomonoff.com/dartmouth/dartprops.jpg.

cards.title: The GENIAC "Electric Brain" Kit
cards.content: The boxed GENIAC "Electric Brain Construction Kit" as preserved in the Computer History Museum: rotary switches, a masonite panel, wire, and bulbs, sold by mail order for $19.95.
cards.significance: Consumer-scale brain hucksterism at the field's birth: the kit's advertising promised a machine that "tests intelligence" and "codes and decodes secret messages" - switch wiring sold to the public as an electric brain.
cards.author: Oliver Garfield Co. (Edmund C. Berkeley, designer)
cards.citation: Computer History Museum, catalog X734.86 (museum record misdates the kit 1950; first sold 1955); advertising text verified in Galaxy Science Fiction, October 1955 (Internet Archive scan)
cards.quote: "GENIAC Electric Brain Construction Kit and spare parts" (catalogue caption)
cards.imageCredit: GENIAC Electric Brain Construction Kit and Spare Parts. 1955. Object, catalog X734.86, Computer History Museum, Mountain View, CA (the museum record misdates the kit 1950; it launched 1955). Accessed November 10, 2026. https://www.computerhistory.org/collections/catalog/X734.86.

cards.title: Wiring Diagrams for an "Electrical Brain"
cards.content: The supplementary wiring-diagram booklet for the GENIAC No. 1 kit, charting the switch circuits behind each advertised "brain machine."
cards.significance: The scam's own schematics: diagram by diagram, the "electrical brain" resolves into rotary switches and flashlight bulbs - the gap between the marketing and the wiring, printed by the seller himself.
cards.author: Oliver Garfield
cards.citation: Oliver Garfield Co., New York, December 1955 (first printing); 16-page scan in the Geniac Document Archive (computercollector.com); physical kit at the Computer History Museum, X734.86
cards.quote: "SUPPLEMENTARY WIRING DIAGRAMS FOR THE GENIAC No.1 ELECTRICAL BRAIN CONSTRUCTION KIT" (title page)
cards.imageCredit: Garfield, Oliver. Supplementary Wiring Diagrams for the Geniac No. 1 Electrical Brain Construction Kit. Title page. New York: Oliver Garfield Co., December 1955. Scans, Geniac Document Archive. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://www.computercollector.com/archive/geniac/.

cards.title: Noel Barber Meets THE BRAIN
cards.content: A London tabloid feature on the IBM 701, presenting the "thought machine" to British readers a month after the Georgetown translation demonstration.
cards.significance: Peak electronic-brain misinformation in the popular press: Frankenstein monsters, a Brain that has "far outstripped the brain of man," thinking "20,000 times faster than any man" - none of it true of the accounting machine it described.
cards.author: Noel Barber
cards.citation: Daily Mail (London), February 6, 1954; full transcription in the Machine Translation Archive (ACL Anthology); page image in Gale's Daily Mail Historical Archive
cards.quote: "the world of tomorrow, the world of Frankenstein monsters, or think-machines whose impulses obey the every whim of man"
cards.imageCredit: Barber, Noel. "Noel Barber Meets THE BRAIN." Daily Mail (London), February 6, 1954. Transcription, Machine Translation Archive via the ACL Anthology. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://aclanthology.org/www.mt-archive.info/DailyMail-1954-Barber.pdf.

cards.title: Zeldner Translates the 23rd Psalm
cards.content: A Hebrew scholar's letter to the New York Herald Tribune demonstrating what word-for-word machine translation would actually produce, preserved verbatim in Warren Weaver's memorandum of that July.
cards.significance: A correction in the Poe tradition: against the "electronic brain translation" stories of 1949, Zeldner simply ran the method by hand on the 23rd Psalm - and the Lord became "Lord my shepherd no I will lack."
cards.author: Max Zeldner
cards.citation: New York Herald Tribune, June 13, 1949; quoted verbatim in Weaver, "Translation" (July 15, 1949), Machine Translation Archive (ACL Anthology); originals in the Warren Weaver papers, Rockefeller Archive Center
cards.quote: "Lord my shepherd no I will lack" (as quoted in Warren Weaver's memorandum of July 15, 1949)
cards.imageCredit: Weaver, Warren. "Translation." Memorandum reproducing Max Zeldner's letter to the New York Herald Tribune of June 13, 1949. Carlsbad, NM, July 15, 1949. Machine Translation Archive via the ACL Anthology. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://aclanthology.org/www.mt-archive.info/Weaver-1949.pdf.

cards.title: Weaver's Diary: Managing Wiener's Doubts
cards.content: A dated entry in Weaver's official Rockefeller Foundation diary, recording a phone call about the preface to the first machine-translation book.
cards.significance: The record being managed in the hype year: Wiener, the field's most famous skeptic, now objects to his own published doubts, and Weaver maps "a course of action, designed to bring Norbert around" - skepticism quietly edited out of the story.
cards.author: Warren Weaver (Rockefeller Foundation officer's diary)
cards.citation: Rockefeller Foundation records, Officers' Diaries, RG 12, Rockefeller Archive Center; 1954 volume fully digitized (dimes.rockarch.org), entry at p. 163
cards.quote: "Norbert Weiner objects to this quotation since he has now changed his mind. We map out a course of action, designed to bring Norbert around to a reasonable position, and it later turns out that this succeeds." (entry of November 17, 1954; "Weiner" is the diary typist's spelling of Wiener)
cards.imageCredit: Weaver, Warren. Officer's diary, 1954, p. 163 (entry of November 17, 1954). Rockefeller Foundation records, Officers' Diaries, RG 12, Rockefeller Archive Center. Digitized volume. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://dimes.rockarch.org/objects/ezoHvQyCTFTdbGPfEXMrqi.

cards.title: Heuristic Problem Solving: The Next Advance in Operations Research
cards.content: A banquet address to the Operations Research Society of America in Pittsburgh, published in the society's journal.
cards.significance: Here Simon predicted that within ten years a computer would be chess champion of the world and would prove an important new theorem - the era's boldest public timetable, rebuked in print by Richard Bellman in the same journal.
cards.author: Herbert A. Simon
cards.citation: Operations Research 6(1):1-10 (1958), INFORMS; Herbert A. Simon Collection, Carnegie Mellon University Archives
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "That within ten years a digital computer will be the world's chess champion, unless the rules bar it from competition."
cards.imageCredit: Herbert A. Simon and Allen Newell Chess Match. 1958. Photograph, photographer unknown; uploaded to Flickr by Paolo Massa. Public domain. Wikimedia Commons. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f7/Herbert_A._Simon_and_Allen_Newell_Chess_Match.jpg.

cards.title: Language and Machines: The ALPAC Report
cards.content: An advisory-committee report to the National Research Council assessing the state and prospects of machine translation and computational linguistics.
cards.significance: Its negative verdict ended most US government machine-translation funding - the first time a sponsor's report switched a computing-with-language field off, and the template for the AI winters to come.
cards.author: Automatic Language Processing Advisory Committee (John R. Pierce, chair)
cards.citation: National Academy of Sciences - National Research Council, Publication 1416 (1966); National Academies Press record 9547
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "we do not have useful machine translation. Further, there is no immediate or predictable prospect of useful machine translation."
cards.imageCredit: Automatic Language Processing Advisory Committee. Language and Machines: Computers in Translation and Linguistics. Title page. Publication 1416. Washington, DC: National Academy of Sciences-National Research Council, 1966. Scan, ACL Anthology. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://aclanthology.org/www.mt-archive.info/ALPAC-1966.pdf.

cards.title: McCarthy at the Chess Console
cards.content: A photograph of John McCarthy seated at the console of Stanford's IBM 7090, testing a computer chess program.
cards.significance: Chess was the proving ground of the era's promises: Simon's ten-year prophecy, Dreyfus's ridicule, and MIT's MacHack VI - which defeated Dreyfus himself in 1967 - all played out over the board.
cards.author: Unrecorded photographer (courtesy Stanford University)
cards.citation: Computer History Museum, accession L062302006, courtesy Stanford University; the 1967 Dreyfus-vs-MacHack game tape is CHM catalog 102689842
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "John McCarthy, artificial intelligence pioneer, playing chess at Stanford's IBM 7090" (catalogue caption)
cards.imageCredit: John McCarthy, Artificial Intelligence Pioneer, Playing Chess at Stanford's IBM 7090. Ca. 1967. Photograph, courtesy of Stanford University. "Mastering the Game" exhibition, Computer History Museum, Mountain View, CA. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://www.computerhistory.org/chess/stl-431e1a07ca980/.

cards.title: ARPANET Logical Map, March 1977
cards.content: A network map locating every host and IMP on the ARPANET as of March 1977 - 111 host computers from MIT and Stanford to the Pentagon.
cards.significance: Nearly every AI laboratory sits on this map as a node: the ARPA-funded network that carried the era's code, data, and people out of individual labs into a national infrastructure.
cards.author: Bolt Beranek and Newman Inc.
cards.citation: ARPANET Completion Report (Bolt Beranek and Newman, January 4, 1978), map plate; related BBN/ARPANET materials in the Computer History Museum
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "ARPANET LOGICAL MAP, MARCH 1977" (printed on the map)
cards.imageCredit: Bolt Beranek and Newman Inc. ARPANET Logical Map, March 1977. 1977. Map plate from the ARPANET Completion Report (1978). Public domain. Wikimedia Commons, source Computer History Museum. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/bf/Arpanet_logical_map%2C_march_1977.png.

cards.title: New Navy Device Learns By Doing
cards.content: A news report on the Navy's demonstration of Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron, which taught itself in fifty trials to tell marked cards apart.
cards.significance: The story relayed Navy claims that the machine would one day walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence - the era's defining specimen of press amplification of a researcher's promises.
cards.author: Byline unrecorded (UPI dispatch)
cards.citation: The New York Times, July 8, 1958, p. 25; NYT TimesMachine
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "will be able to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence"
cards.imageCredit: Hay, John C., and Albert E. Murray. "Mark I Perceptron." Figure 2 in Mark I Perceptron Operators' Manual, 1960. Public domain. Wikimedia Commons. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/13/Mark_I_Perceptron%2C_Figure_2_of_operator%27s_manual.png.

cards.title: The Intergalactic Computer Network Memo
cards.content: An internal ARPA memorandum from Licklider to his funded investigators about coordinating their research and linking their computing projects.
cards.significance: The patron's own working memo: ARPA money deliberately knitting the early AI and computing centers into a community, sketching the networked vision ARPA would later fund into the ARPANET.
cards.author: J.C.R. Licklider
cards.citation: ARPA memorandum, Washington DC, April 23, 1963; reproduced from ARPA/IPTO records; full text republished by KurzweilAI.net (2001)
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "It seems to me to be interesting and important, nevertheless, to develop a capability for integrated network operation."
cards.imageCredit: J. C. R. Licklider. N.d. Photograph, photographer unknown. Public domain (via the U.S. National Library of Medicine). Wikimedia Commons. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/66/J._C._R._Licklider.jpg.

cards.title: Harold Cohen's Notebook 3
cards.content: One of Cohen's dated working notebooks, with sketches of mazes grown stage by stage - early workings behind his drawing program AARON.
cards.significance: The day-by-day record of an artist teaching a computer to draw; AARON went on to exhibit from Documenta to the Brooklyn Museum - the era's successes reaching beyond the laboratory into art.
cards.author: Harold Cohen
cards.citation: Collection of the Harold Cohen Trust; exhibited in "Harold Cohen: AARON," Whitney Museum of American Art, 2024
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "Artist's sketch for Mazes that are grown incrementally, with numbers representing the stage of each maze element" (exhibition label)
cards.imageCredit: Cohen, Harold. 0305-03. 2003. Digital inkjet print. Museum no. 2010EL6973, Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O114802/.

cards.title: The General Purpose Robot is a Mirage
cards.content: A televised Royal Institution debate in which the author of a government-commissioned review of AI defends his conclusions against John McCarthy, Donald Michie, and Richard Gregory.
cards.significance: The first winter arriving on national television: the report behind this debate precipitated Britain's deep cuts to AI research - the era's promises called to account. The full 81-minute recording survives.
cards.author: Sir James Lighthill
cards.citation: Recording preserved by AIAI, University of Edinburgh (BBC broadcast, June 1973); Lighthill's report Artificial Intelligence: A General Survey (1972) hosted alongside
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "In no part of the field have the discoveries made so far produced the major impact that was then promised."
cards.imageCredit: Lighthill, James, John McCarthy, Donald Michie, and Richard Gregory. The Lighthill Debate. 1973. Video recording (BBC "Controversy"; still frame). Artificial Intelligence Applications Institute, University of Edinburgh. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://www.aiai.ed.ac.uk/events/lighthill1973/.

cards.title: The MYCIN Dissertation
cards.content: A Stanford doctoral dissertation describing a rule-based consultation program that recommends antibiotic therapy for blood infections.
cards.significance: A late-era success that seeded the next boom: MYCIN set the template for the expert-systems industry, and a 1979 evaluation showed its advice matching Stanford specialists - yet it was never deployed on the wards.
cards.author: Edward H. Shortliffe
cards.citation: Stanford University Ph.D. dissertation (degree 1975); issued as Stanford AI Laboratory Memo AIM-251 / STAN-CS-74-465; published as Computer-Based Medical Consultations: MYCIN (Elsevier, 1976)
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "This system, termed MYCIN, utilizes computer techniques derived principally from the subfield of computer science known as artificial intelligence (AI). MYCIN's task is to assist with the decisions involved in the selection of appropriate therapy for patients with infections." (preface to the 1976 published edition)
cards.imageCredit: Shortliffe, Edward H. Computer-Based Medical Consultations: MYCIN. Cover. New York: Elsevier, 1976. Cover image via Google Books. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://books.google.com/books/content?id=i9QXugPQw6oC&printsec=frontcover&img=1&zoom=1.

cards.title: Shakey the Robot
cards.content: A photographic print of Stanford Research Institute's mobile robot Shakey in its experimental environment.
cards.significance: Shakey was the first mobile robot to reason about its own actions, integrating perception, planning, and action - the era's most photogenic success, and a lightning rod for its critics.
cards.author: Unrecorded photographer (SRI)
cards.citation: Computer History Museum, catalog 102695825, accession X3501.2006; the robot itself is CHM lot X279.83, gift of SRI International
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "Experimental Mobile Automaton ("Shakey")" (catalogue caption)
cards.imageCredit: "The wub." SRI Shakey Robot, 1969, Computer History Museum. 2023. Photograph. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c3/SRI_Shakey_robot%2C_1969%2C_Computer_History_Museum.jpg.

cards.title: Map of Shakey's Experimental Environment
cards.content: A plan of the rooms, doorways, and corridors of the robot's test environment at SRI, printed in the project's summary technical report.
cards.significance: The expose half of the "electronic person" story: while LIFE told readers a machine person had arrived, the person's entire world was a few bare rooms of painted blocks - this map is what the headlines actually described.
cards.author: Nils J. Nilsson, ed. (SRI)
cards.citation: "Shakey the Robot," SRI AI Center Technical Note 323 (April 1984); copies at SRI and the Computer History Museum (catalog 102659872)
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "MAP OF SHAKEY'S EXPERIMENTAL ENVIRONMENT" (figure title)
cards.imageCredit: "Map of Shakey's Experimental Environment." In Nils J. Nilsson, ed., Shakey the Robot, Technical Note 323. Menlo Park, CA: SRI International Artificial Intelligence Center, 1984. Document record: catalog 102659872, Computer History Museum. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://www.computerhistory.org/collections/catalog/102659872.

cards.title: Meet Shaky, the First Electronic Person
cards.content: A LIFE magazine feature - a weekly national magazine, not a daily paper - presenting SRI's robot as "the first electronic person" and quoting Marvin Minsky on the imminence of human-level machines.
cards.significance: The canonical AI-hype artifact: the three-to-eight-years "general intelligence" quotation, which Minsky and SRI both disputed, defined public misinformation about the field for a decade and shadowed it into the funding winter.
cards.author: Brad Darrach
cards.citation: LIFE 69, no. 21 (November 20, 1970); issue scan via Google Books (Internet Archive mirror bub_gb_2FMEAAAAMBAJ)
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "In from three to eight years we will have a machine with the general intelligence of an average human being." (Minsky, as quoted; he later disputed the quotation)
cards.imageCredit: Darrach, Brad. "Meet Shaky, the First Electronic Person." LIFE 69, no. 21 (November 20, 1970). Issue scan via Google Books / Internet Archive. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_2FMEAAAAMBAJ.

cards.title: Whither Speech Recognition?
cards.content: A published letter to the editor of the Journal of the Acoustical Society of America by Bell Labs' communications chief, attacking the claims made for automatic speech recognition.
cards.significance: An insider charging the field itself with charlatanism - glamour and deceit sold to funding agencies - in the era's most quoted accusation of scientific hucksterism; Bell Labs' own speech-recognition work stopped for a decade.
cards.author: John R. Pierce
cards.citation: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 46(4B):1049-1051 (October 1969), DOI 10.1121/1.1911801; quoted contemporaneously in a Stanford AI Laboratory draft reply of November 29, 1969 (SAILDART archive)
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "To sell suckers, one uses deceit and offers glamor." (as quoted in a contemporaneous Stanford AI Laboratory reply)
cards.imageCredit: Pierce, John R. "Whither Speech Recognition?" Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 46, no. 4B (October 1969): 1049-1051. DOI 10.1121/1.1911801. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://pubs.aip.org/jasa/article/46/4B/1049/746573/.

cards.title: McCorduck's Journal: Testing the Debunker
cards.content: A dated journal entry written after interviewing Hubert Dreyfus, the field's most prominent debunker, for the history of AI she was writing.
cards.significance: False leads cut both ways: the era's chief claim-checker, pressed politely on his own published claims, concedes on the spot that some cannot be defended - a working chronicler's record of how fragile both sides' certainties were.
cards.author: Pamela McCorduck
cards.citation: Pamela McCorduck's journals, Carnegie Mellon University Archives, Hunt Library (currently closed to researchers); entry in This Could Be Important (ETC Press, 2019)
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "I'd come to grips with his objections, that I understood them, raised questions about them, which, to my astonishment, he couldn't answer: "Yes, that's weak," "No, I don't have an answer for that."" (entry of July 21, 1976)
cards.imageCredit: McCorduck, Pamela. Journal entry of July 21, 1976. In This Could Be Important: My Life and Times with the Artificial Intelligentsia. Pittsburgh: ETC Press, 2019.

cards.title: The Twenty-Years Prophecy
cards.content: The third of Simon's 1960 lectures on the new science of management decision, published the same year, predicting the full automation of human work.
cards.significance: The era's boldest false prophecy, from one of its most rigorous scientists: machines doing "any work that a man can do" within twenty years - a claim repeated for decades as evidence of what the field had promised and not delivered.
cards.author: Herbert A. Simon
cards.citation: Simon, The New Science of Management Decision (Harper, 1960), Lecture III, p. 38; wording sourced via Quote Investigator
cards.era: Early Successes and the First Winter, 1957-1977
cards.quote: "machines will be capable, within twenty years, of doing any work that a man can do"
cards.imageCredit: Simon, Herbert A. The New Science of Management Decision. New York: Harper and Brothers, 1960 (The Ford Distinguished Lectures; quotation at p. 38, sourced via Quote Investigator). Accessed November 10, 2026. https://quoteinvestigator.com/2020/11/11/ai-can-do/.

cards.title: Minds, Brains, and Programs
cards.content: A target article in a peer-commentary journal presenting an argument that an appropriately programmed computer does not thereby have cognitive states.
cards.significance: The second cycle opens with its sharpest critique: the most-debated attack on strong AI ever published, carrying 27 rebuttals from the builders and Searle's reply inside itself - a complete debate in one artifact.
cards.author: John R. Searle
cards.citation: Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3(3):417-457 (1980), Cambridge University Press; DOI 10.1017/S0140525X00005756
cards.quote: "no program by itself is sufficient for thinking"
cards.imageCredit: Breindel, Matthew. John Searle. 2005. Photograph. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/69/John_searle2.jpg.

cards.title: The Parallel Inference Machines
cards.content: Photographs of the PIM/p and PIM/m parallel inference machines, the final hardware of Japan's Fifth Generation project.
cards.significance: What eleven years and 54 billion yen of ministry patronage physically bought: prototype machines that were museum pieces, not market products, by the project's close.
cards.author: ICOT (photographs via the IPSJ Computer Museum)
cards.citation: IPSJ Computer Museum online catalogue; the machines are preserved at the National Museum of Nature and Science, Tokyo
cards.quote: "five PIM models were produced, including the PIM/p comprised of 512 constituent processors, and the PIM/m comprised of 256 constituent processors"
cards.imageCredit: Parallel Inference Machines PIM/p and PIM/m. Photographs. IPSJ Computer Museum, Information Processing Society of Japan. Accessed November 10, 2026. http://museum.ipsj.or.jp/computer/other/images/0002_01.gif.

cards.title: Moscow Ballistic Missile Defense
cards.content: A Defense Department map, reproduced in a congressional assessment, locating the components of the Soviet anti-missile system around Moscow.
cards.significance: The report around this map framed Congress's doubts that tens of millions of lines of battle-management software could ever be trusted - the boom's defense patronage meeting its deepest technical dissent.
cards.author: US Department of Defense (in US Congress, OTA)
cards.citation: US Congress, Office of Technology Assessment, Ballistic Missile Defense Technologies, OTA-ISC-254 (GPO, September 1985), pp. 60-61; archived at the UNT CyberCemetery
cards.quote: "The Moscow ballistic missile defenses identified in the map at right include the Pushkino ABM radar"
cards.imageCredit: U.S. Department of Defense. "Moscow Ballistic Missile Defense." Map. In U.S. Congress, Office of Technology Assessment, Ballistic Missile Defense Technologies, OTA-ISC-254, 60. Washington, DC: U.S. Government Printing Office, 1985. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://govinfo.library.unt.edu/ota/Ota_4/DATA/1985/8504.PDF.

cards.title: 'Fifth Generation' Became Japan's Lost Generation
cards.content: A news report on Japan's conclusion of its ten-year Fifth Generation computer project, with the government offering the project's software to any taker.
cards.significance: The dated obituary for the project that set off the 1980s funding race: after some 400 million dollars of ministry money, the sponsor walked away - the second winter announced on the business page.
cards.author: Andrew Pollack
cards.citation: The New York Times, June 5, 1992, Section D, p. 1 (National edition); NYT archive
cards.quote: "A bold 10-year effort by Japan to seize the lead in computer technology is fizzling to a close, having failed to meet many of its ambitious goals or to produce technology that Japan's computer industry wanted."
cards.imageCredit: Pollack, Andrew. "'Fifth Generation' Became Japan's Lost Generation." New York Times, June 5, 1992, D1. Printed page as reproduced in TimesMachine. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1992/06/05/864692.html.

cards.title: Selling the Fifth Generation
cards.content: A typed letter from McCorduck to Edward Feigenbaum laying out how to pitch their book on Japan's Fifth Generation project to New York publishers.
cards.significance: The genesis document of The Fifth Generation (1983), the book that carried the Japanese challenge to Washington and helped trigger the decade's funding race - the boom's rhetoric visible in draft.
cards.author: Pamela McCorduck
cards.citation: Edward A. Feigenbaum Papers, SC0340, Box 37, Folder 5, Stanford University Special Collections; digitized scan at purl.stanford.edu/nd130tf3379
cards.quote: "We offer a hellish vision of what will happen if this opportunity isn't snatched away from the Japanese, but we also offer a celestial vision of what can happen if we meet the challenge."
cards.imageCredit: McCorduck, Pamela. Letter to Edward A. Feigenbaum, January 19, 1982. Digitized scan. Edward A. Feigenbaum Papers, SC0340, Box 37, Folder 5, Stanford University Special Collections. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://purl.stanford.edu/nd130tf3379.

cards.title: McCorduck's Journal: A Banquet in Tokyo
cards.content: A dated journal entry describing the banquet of Japan's Fifth Generation conference in Tokyo, attended with Edward Feigenbaum.
cards.significance: A same-night private record from inside the peak of the Fifth Generation boom, by the co-author of the 1983 book that stoked the West's funding alarm.
cards.author: Pamela McCorduck
cards.citation: Pamela McCorduck's journals, Carnegie Mellon University Archives, Hunt Library (currently closed to researchers); entry in This Could Be Important (ETC Press, 2019)
cards.quote: "An elegant French-style banquet, and I'm asked to say a few words. I talk about the momentous occasion not only for Japan, but for the human race."
cards.imageCredit: "Edward Feigenbaum (Center), Director of the Stanford University Computation Center in 1996." Photograph. In Pamela McCorduck, This Could Be Important, photo gallery. Pittsburgh: ETC Press, 2019.

cards.title: The Dark Ages of AI
cards.content: The published record of a panel at the 1984 national AI conference in Austin on whether inflated expectations could collapse the field's support.
cards.significance: The moment the field named its own fear - "AI winter," borrowed from nuclear winter - on its own stage, four years before the funding actually fell.
cards.author: Drew McDermott, Roger Schank, and panel
cards.citation: AI Magazine 6(3):122-134 (Fall 1985), AAAI; panel held at AAAI-84, Austin, Texas
cards.quote: "there's a mood that I'm sure many of you are familiar with of deep unease among AI researchers who have been around more than the last four years or so. This unease is due to the worry that perhaps expectations about AI are too high, and that this will eventually result in disaster."
cards.imageCredit: McDermott, Drew, M. Mitchell Waldrop, B. Chandrasekaran, John McDermott, and Roger Schank. "The Dark Ages of AI: A Panel Discussion at AAAI-84." First page. AI Magazine 6, no. 3 (Fall 1985): 122-134. CC BY. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://ojs.aaai.org/aimagazine/index.php/aimagazine/article/view/494.

cards.title: Strategic Computing
cards.content: DARPA's ten-year plan proposing a major program to develop machine-intelligence technology and apply it to critical defense problems.
cards.significance: The American answer to Japan: roughly a billion dollars of new defense money that funded the expert-systems boom - and whose redirection after 1987 helped precipitate the second winter.
cards.author: Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency
cards.citation: DARPA, Washington DC, October 28, 1983; Defense Technical Information Center, accession ADA141982
cards.quote: "the Agency plans to create a new generation of "machine intelligence technology.""
cards.imageCredit: Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. Strategic Computing: New-Generation Computing Technology. Cover. Washington, DC: DARPA, October 28, 1983. DTIC ADA141982; cover image via Internet Archive. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://archive.org/services/img/DTIC_ADA141982.

cards.title: The Deep Blue Team, Match Night
cards.content: A photograph of the IBM Deep Blue development team taken after the final game of the 1997 rematch in New York.
cards.significance: The cycle's end beyond the winter: hours after a computer first beat a reigning world champion under tournament conditions, corporate R&D - not government patronage - delivered AI's most famous public victory.
cards.author: Unrecorded photographer (from Feng-hsiung Hsu)
cards.citation: Computer History Museum, catalog 102645318, accession X3306.2006, gift of Feng-hsiung Hsu
cards.quote: "In May 1997, IBM supercomputer Deep Blue played World Chess Champion Garry Kasparov winning the six-game rematch 3.5-2.5." (catalogue caption)
cards.imageCredit: Deep Blue Team after 1997 Deep Blue vs. Kasparov Re-match in New York City, New York. May 11, 1997. Photograph, photographer unrecorded; gift of Feng-hsiung Hsu. Catalog 102645318, Computer History Museum, Mountain View, CA. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://www.computerhistory.org/collections/catalog/102645318.

cards.title: The NSFNET Backbone, September 1991
cards.content: A three-dimensional visualization map of the United States showing one month of traffic flowing into the NSFNET T1 backbone.
cards.significance: What the research network built by AI's patrons had become by the second winter: the NSFNET that succeeded the ARPANET, visualized at NCSA just as the Internet eclipsed the field that seeded it.
cards.author: Donna Cox and Robert Patterson (NCSA); data by Merit Network
cards.citation: Donna Cox and Robert Patterson, NCSA, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, with Merit Network data; reproduced in the CAIDA Internet Atlas, UC San Diego
cards.quote: "a visualization study of inbound traffic measured in billions of bytes on the NSFNET T1 backbone for September 1991" (credit caption)
cards.imageCredit: Cox, Donna, and Robert Patterson. NSFNET T1 Backbone and Regional Networks, September 1991. Traffic visualization; data by Merit Network, Inc. NCSA, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. CAIDA Internet Atlas. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://www.caida.org/projects/internetatlas/gallery/nsfnet/1457.cox.lg.gif.

cards.title: Can Machines Think? Humans Match Wits
cards.content: The New York Times front-page report of the first Loebner Prize Turing-test contest at the Boston Computer Museum, where a chatbot's trick conversation fooled half the judges.
cards.significance: A conversation program "programmed to make whimsical conversation" fooled five of ten judges and made page one as historic news - deception by design, reported as a milestone; the contest's own museum report preserves the numbers.
cards.author: John Markoff
cards.citation: The New York Times, November 9, 1991, p. 1 (continued p. 10); the event documented in The Computer Museum News (Winter 1992), scan hosted by the Computer History Museum
cards.quote: "The judges typed questions into computer terminals and tried to decide from the responses whether they were communicating with a man or a machine. One program proved convincing enough to fool 5 of the 10 judges."
cards.imageCredit: Markoff, John. "Can Machines Think? Humans Match Wits." New York Times, November 9, 1991, 1 (continued p. 10). Printed page as reproduced in TimesMachine. Accessed November 10, 2026.

cards.title: Computers in Your Future: An Exchange
cards.content: A published exchange in the New York Review of Books: the authors of The Fifth Generation protest Weizenbaum's review of their book, and Weizenbaum replies.
cards.significance: A fight about misinformation at the boom's crest: Weizenbaum's review had charged the bestseller with hype and "references to nonexistent documents," and his reply to the authors' protest gave no ground.
cards.author: Edward A. Feigenbaum, Pamela McCorduck, and Joseph Weizenbaum
cards.citation: The New York Review of Books, December 8, 1983; full text at nybooks.com; the review under dispute ran October 27, 1983
cards.quote: "No, the review was sufficiently merited by the book; no other factors were needed." (Weizenbaum's reply)
cards.imageCredit: "Computers in Your Future." Letters: Edward A. Feigenbaum and Pamela McCorduck, with Joseph Weizenbaum's reply. New York Review of Books, December 8, 1983. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1983/12/08/computers-in-your-future/.

cards.title: McCorduck's Journal: A Rumor at Stanford
cards.content: A dated journal entry recording, secondhand from a Yorktown Heights researcher, the graduate-student folklore then circulating about who really wrote The Fifth Generation.
cards.significance: Misinformation moving through the field itself, caught in a diary as it spread: a false claim about the boom's most famous book, each retelling (the entry notes) growing taller and farther from fact.
cards.author: Pamela McCorduck
cards.citation: Pamela McCorduck's journals, Carnegie Mellon University Archives, Hunt Library (currently closed to researchers); entry in This Could Be Important (ETC Press, 2019)
cards.quote: "Everybody knows that Feigenbaum not only didn't write The Fifth Generation, but hardly knows what's in it." (entry of May 21, 1984, recording a campus rumor)
cards.imageCredit: McCorduck, Pamela. Journal entry of May 21, 1984. In This Could Be Important: My Life and Times with the Artificial Intelligentsia. Pittsburgh: ETC Press, 2019.

cards.title: Some Expert Systems Need Common Sense
cards.content: A lecture to the New York Academy of Sciences by AI's co-founder, examining what the celebrated expert systems actually contain.
cards.significance: The field's founder dismantling its sales pitch at the boom's peak: MYCIN's ontology has no doctors, hospitals, illness, or death, and the systems do not know what they do not know - the gap the marketing never mentioned.
cards.author: John McCarthy
cards.citation: Published in Pagels, ed., Computer Culture, Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences 426 (1984): 129-137; author's full text at jmc.stanford.edu
cards.quote: "Doctors, hospitals, illness and death are absent."
cards.imageCredit: McCarthy, John. "Some Expert Systems Need Common Sense." In Computer Culture: The Scientific, Intellectual, and Social Impact of the Computer, ed. Heinz Pagels. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences 426 (1984): 129-137. Author's full text, Stanford University. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://www-formal.stanford.edu/jmc/someneed/someneed.html.

cards.title: The Policeman's Beard Is Half Constructed
cards.content: A Warner Books volume of computer prose and poetry credited to the program Racter and billed on its jacket as the first book ever written by a computer.
cards.significance: A publishing hoax at the boom's height: scholarship later showed the prose depended on heavy human templating and curation, and that the commercial Racter program could not produce the book's output - the claim sold the machine, not the method.
cards.author: William Chamberlain and Thomas Etter ("Racter")
cards.citation: Warner Software/Warner Books, 1984; lending scan at the Internet Archive; the jacket claim and its debunking documented in Henrickson, Electronic Book Review (April 4, 2021)
cards.quote: "the first book ever written by a computer" (jacket claim, as reproduced in scholarship)
cards.imageCredit: Racter (William Chamberlain and Thomas Etter). The Policeman's Beard Is Half Constructed. Cover. New York: Warner Books, 1984. Lending scan, Internet Archive. Accessed November 10, 2026. https://archive.org/details/policemansbeardi0000unse.
